title: Decomposition, reusable functions and interface contracts (CodeSaathi extension)
learningObjectives: Explain the C concept and its rules.
Trace the example and describe data flow.
Identify relevant failure and boundary cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: Program decomposition separates a larger task into functions with clear responsibilities. An interface contract states what inputs are valid, what outputs or side effects are produced, and what errors or ownership rules apply.
understand.whyItMatters: Explicit contracts make functions easier to test, reuse and maintain. They also reduce hidden assumptions between callers and callees.
understand.analogy: Treat the operation as a clearly specified contract between the program and its data.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's type, lifetime, I/O and object representation rules.

explain.narrative:
Program decomposition separates a larger task into functions with clear responsibilities. An interface contract states what inputs are valid, what outputs or side effects are produced, and what errors or ownership rules apply.

Check all return values, object lifetimes, types and preconditions. Enable compiler warnings and test expected as well as failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The function documents its input requirements through checks, writes the result only when the request is valid and reports success with bool. A production contract should also define the permitted value range and overflow policy for sum.

practise.guidedTask: Identify the preconditions, postconditions and failure result.
practise.independentTask: Decompose a small inventory report into input validation, calculation and output functions. Write a contract for each function.
hints: A function contract should state pointer nullability, array count, ownership and mutation.
Keep I/O separate from calculation when that makes the logic easier to test.
Choose return values that distinguish valid results from failure.
